We all remember where we were in that moment when much of the world changed. Thoughts go to those who were lost on that day as we get started into today's Daily Dealer Live. All right. Yesterday, I led a panel at Chempress Supplier Summit, Detroit, Michigan, with four of the best fixed ops leaders in all of automotive. And at the start, I shared a thought I share at almost every keynote I give. The quality of our conversation dictates our ability to overcome challenges and problems in our industry. And what made yesterday especially powerful was that the people sitting in that room, well, they're uniquely positioned to actually solve many of those problems, from the operators on the panel to the participants and attendees in the room, many of whom, by the way, I had no idea existed before I sat in that space. That's the power of a room like that. Thoughtful, high-performing leaders committed to excellence in their craft, willing to challenge how things have always been done. And by the way, they had a little bit of fun along the way. And on that, the panel stopped being a panel. It became a debate. It became a conversation. It became a discussion on why repair orders are declining, whether dealerships should intentionally lose money to retain a customer tomorrow, whether OEM maintenance intervals actually reflect how customers use their vehicles, whether we're losing customers because of the market or because we simply are too difficult to do business with. We talked about older vehicles, tires, video MPIs, mobile service, AI, and we uncovered what I think is a fascinating supply chain problem. We expect parts suppliers to anticipate demand without giving them visibility into that demand data. By the way, a problem I don't think any of us on the panel, myself included, had any idea existed. So when we wrapped yesterday, I wasn't ready to stop that conversation. So today we're bringing that conversation to you. And before we dive into it, we're reminding you we're streaming live across all CDG social media platforms. Post your comments. We'll bring you into today's show through your comments. And before we hit the panel, let's go to today's automotive industry headlines. All right, kicking off today with some major wholesale market news. Get this. Copart is acquiring ACV auctions for $1.9 billion in cash. They're paying about $10.5 per share, about 45% above where ACV was trading before word of the deal broke. ACV will operate as an independent subsidiary under its existing leadership, keeping its own website and brand. Together, the two platforms handle more than 4.8 million vehicles annually. Copart, through its 275-plus physical yards and salvage network, ACV, through its dealer-only digital marketplace with 22,000 active buyers. The deal, the idea is that Copart brings physical scale and international buyer demand, while ACV brings dealer relationships, digital inspections, and valuation tech. For franchise and independent dealers, the combined platform should mean more liquidity options and easier logistics on trade-in consolidation. That's big news to all of our friends at both sides, but in particular to George over there at ACV. Moving on to a useful data point for the sales floor, IC cars analyzed more than 395 million vehicles and found Toyota leads all brands in longevity. Lexus came in second at 14.4%, Honda third at 13.3%, and Acura, well, they're fourth at just under 10%, 9.5%, the only brands with double-digit odds. pending_qa.q: What role does customer friction play in repair order decline compared to market availability?
pending_qa.r: Dave Rogers argues friction accounts for probably 50 percent of the issue, citing that dealers make it very difficult to do business through too many rules of engagement when customers call, poor phone availability, and an attitude of saying no first instead of yes. He emphasizes the need to say yes and find solutions like offering loaner vehicles rather than creating conditions that make customers hang up and go elsewhere.

pending_qa.q: How should dealership service departments answer incoming phone calls to improve customer retention?
pending_qa.r: Richard Lupo advocates for proactive solutions, noting that Apple Tree Automotive uses an AI agent that catches every single call, logs it, and schedules approximately 30 percent of appointments through AI with successful transfers. However, Tully Williams counters that he wants to maintain human-to-human contact during business hours, reserving AI for after-hours options, stating the dealership has been in business for 105 years and customers prefer talking to people rather than robots.

pending_qa.q: What percentage of routine vehicle service will migrate to mobile service outside dealership locations?
pending_qa.r: Ed Roberts predicted that within five years, 60 percent of service visits will be mobile. Richard Lupo estimates 50 percent of routine maintenance like oil changes and tire rotations will be done outside the brick-and-mortar facility within a few short years. Dave Rogers agrees that customers would accept this split, saying if dealers meet customers halfway on 50 percent of the work, customers will give them the other 50 percent.

pending_qa.q: Should dealerships prioritize gaining more customer demand or eliminating customer friction in service operations?
pending_qa.r: Dave Rogers and Tully Williams both chose 20 percent more demand, with Tully noting he would turn increased demand into no friction anyway. Richard Lupo chose zero customer friction, arguing that if you create that experience, the business will build naturally. Sam Dark challenged Dave and Tully by asking why the market should give dealerships more customers if their current friction levels are leaking customers to the aftermarket.

pending_qa.q: How has OEM data sharing with parts suppliers impacted automotive parts availability in dealerships?
pending_qa.r: The panel discovered a significant supply chain problem: OEMs are not supplying their part suppliers with visibility into sales data, forcing suppliers to anticipate demand without that critical information. Dave Rogers found it fascinating that companies have extensive data but don't aggregate it for usefulness, leaving suppliers unable to know parts availability. Tully Williams noted that parts suppliers are asking OEMs to simply give them the data so they can better anticipate part needs.

pending_qa.q: Should dealerships follow OEM-recommended maintenance intervals or adopt more frequent service schedules?
pending_qa.r: Tully Williams was the sole dissenter on the panel, believing the factory should dictate maintenance intervals and dealerships should stay by those factory standards. The other three guests advocated for more advanced rotation schedules, such as oil changes every six months, whereas Tully's manufacturers predominantly recommend one-year intervals. Tully emphasized the importance of adhering to factory standards set by OEM engineers.
